prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate economic fluctuations, providing the theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part for B002, credited to Kiyotaki and Moore. The merit case rests on three things. First, the 1997 paper is an original and tractable general-equilibrium mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values create a feedback loop between asset prices and credit, so temporary shocks become large and persistent. Second, it has about thirty years of absorption into macro-finance, quantitative macro and central-bank modelling, so maturity is not in question. Third, credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, with a two-author founding paper and no contested split. The exchange sharpened my view on two points. The chair summary shows that no member argues against the Kiyotaki-Moore core and that most members decline to add Gertler. I do not count that as scientific merit. What persuades me is the reasoning: Gertler's best-known work belongs to the accelerator lineage, which runs through an existing laureate, and to intermediary-based models that are a broader and different achievement. His credit is also split with B043. On the chair's overlap question, my principle is a distinct-discovery test. Adjacency to a recent prize is a timing and balance consideration for the Committee, not a merit criterion. It becomes decisive only if the new work is substantially the same discovery. Applied consistently, 2022 versus B002, 2008 versus B025 and 2024 versus B050 and B021 are all cases of neighbouring mechanisms, not duplication. That is why the overlap lowers my confidence in B002 but does not change my ranking. On the chair's evidence question, I would accept firm-level and household-level studies showing investment, borrowing or spending responding to exogenous variation in collateral values, and quantitative models disciplined by such moments. I recall such studies but have not verified them here, and nothing in the record changes my ordering on this point.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig is the main risk. I treat the collateral and asset-price mechanism as separable from bank runs and intermediation, but that is a judgment, not a settled fact. The empirical identification of the quantitative size of collateral-driven amplification is weaker than the theory's influence suggests, and the quantitative literature disagrees on the magnitude. A two-name citation also leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, so a reader of the financial-accelerator literature could find it incomplete. Finally, I am a macroeconomist working near this area, so I may overweight a mechanism that serves as a building block for models I use. I discount that, and it is one reason I keep B025 and B012 as live alternatives and do not treat B002 as the only defensible outcome.

responses.point: Hassler keeps Gertler as a third name. He argues that Gertler's later intermediary-based quantitative work with Kiyotaki and with Karadi is separable from the 2022 recognition and connects to the collateral-constraint mechanism. He accepts Kiyotaki and Moore alone as a fallback.
responses.response: I take the separation argument seriously, and I agree that the intermediary-based models are not the same as the 2022 work on runs and banking. My difficulty is the opposite one. That work is a distinct and broader achievement, namely financial intermediaries in macro models. It is not part of the discovery of the 1997 collateral mechanism, so naming it in this citation widens the scope beyond the originating paper. It also brings back the accelerator lineage, and Gertler's credit is shared with B043. I read his two-name fallback as the stronger version of his own case. If the Committee wants to recognise intermediary-based macro-finance, that is a different citation with a different set of names, which could include Gilchrist and others, and it should be judged on its own record. I would not block a three-name B002 if it were the only route to a decision, but I would regard it as the weaker prize.

responses.point: Teorell proposes two parts, B002 for Kiyotaki and Moore and B012 for Pakes alone. He uses the three-person cap to drop Gertler, and he records that omitting Berry and Levinsohn is a real attribution loss.
responses.response: I agree with him on dropping Gertler and on keeping B002 to the two originators. I do not support the combination as my preferred configuration, for two reasons. The first is attribution: Pakes alone credits the BLP programme to one person and omits Berry and Levinsohn, which Teorell himself describes as a real loss. The second is thematic, since a prize pairing macro-finance with empirical IO has no common discovery. Neither reason is a merit judgment against Pakes, whose dynamic-games and estimation work I respect. My vote does not depend on a second part, and the cap would force an attribution compromise I would rather not make in order to fill a second slot. I would weigh the combination on its merits if it were the only configuration able to command a majority, but I do not propose it.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B012 first. She answers the tools-versus-discovery concern by arguing that BLP is a measurement framework with identifiable economic content, recovering elasticities, markups and welfare effects. She names B002 as her main fallback.
responses.response: Her point is fair and moves me a little, since measurement that changes what regulators and researchers can credibly conclude is a discovery in its own right. I still weigh B002 above B012 for two reasons. Kiyotaki-Moore has a single identifiable origin, while the BLP credit is spread over a larger group, and Bresnahan, Benkard and Levin remain open questions. Her own note that no three-person set around BLP would be fully defensible if Bresnahan were judged equal in kind is the main reason. B012 stays among my alternatives, and I would regard it as a respectable outcome. My ordering reflects the cleanliness of credit more than a view that conceptual mechanisms outrank methods.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B050 and answered my round-1 concerns. He accepts the identification point, argues that the 2024 prize is adjacent but not duplicative, and keeps Besley because the state-capacity strand extends the framework to development.
responses.response: I agree that the 2024 institutions prize concerns a different mechanism and outcome, and that adjacency is not duplication, which is the same principle I apply to B002. I accept his case for the state-capacity strand as extending the work beyond rich-country electoral rules. My remaining difference is about evidence. He concedes that the cross-country identification is thinner than the theory's influence. The identification of collateral amplification is also imperfect, but B002 has a more precisely stated mechanism and a clearer origin, and the credit in B050 is more contestable, as he notes of Besley. I keep B050 outside my alternatives, which are limited to two. I regard it as a coherent programme and would not call support for it unreasonable.

uncertainties: How much of the credit-cycle mechanism the Committee regards as already covered by the 2022 banking and financial-crisis prize.
Whether the empirical evidence supports quantitatively large collateral amplification, which I cannot verify from the supplied materials.
Whether leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist makes the citation look incomplete relative to the financial-accelerator literature. I have not independently verified how that literature divides credit.

Whether, on a fuller attribution review, B025 or B012 is the stronger fallback if the 2022 overlap proves decisive. B025 has the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum gap and the 2008 adjacency, and B012 has the Bresnahan, Benkard and Levin gap.
Whether the Committee would prefer a configuration with a second part in order to reach a majority. I have not found one that I can support without a real attribution cost.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent with the B002 credited names, since Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler and Gilchrist are not among the co-authors in my profile. I disclose long-term co-authorship with John Hassler (chair) and Timo Boppart (co-opted member). Both are colleagues, not candidates, and both prefer B002. I do not treat their agreement with me as independent confirmation of merit. My research in heterogeneous-agent and quantitative macro is adjacent to macro-finance, and I do not treat that as a conflict. Several profile co-authors, such as Violante, Ríos-Rull, Smith, Greenwood, Hercowitz, Tsyvinski and Olovsson, are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. No other connection to the credited names on B025, B012 or the other shortlisted ballots is apparent from the supplied profile. No conflict is adjudicated.
